lines: Close the hatch on a hundred and
forty-five people,
dive, and from that moment every breath
they take changes the air they have left.
So what keeps them alive down there — for
weeks,
even months — without coming up?
This is a nuclear-powered submarine. Many
navies use diesel-electric boats,
which work very differently — so
everything here describes a nuclear one.
Once it's submerged, its air goes round in
a closed loop.
Nothing comes in from outside.
US ballistic-missile submarines spend, on
average,
seventy-seven days at sea per patrol. For
all that time,
the boat has to protect, clean and supply
everyone inside.
The first threat presses in from outside.
Every ten metres of seawater adds roughly
another atmosphere of pressure — another
full weight of air pushing on every
surface.
The part of the submarine that holds that
back is the pressure hull:
a round steel tube, braced by rings of
steel frames.
Engineers design it so the shell can't
buckle inward or crumple.
How deep real submarines can go isn't
published
so the depths here are a scale, not a
specification.
That steel keeps the ocean out — and seals
the crew in with their own air.
And that air fails in two separate ways.
Oxygen gets used up.
And carbon dioxide builds up — the biggest
source on board is the crew's own breath.
Making more oxygen doesn't take carbon
dioxide away,
so the submarine needs a different machine
for each problem.
Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, and it
can collect in enclosed spaces.
At high enough concentrations it causes
breathlessness and headaches,
and at extreme levels, unconsciousness.
So it's removed continuously. Air is
pushed through a scrubber containing an
amine — a chemical that grabs carbon
dioxide. Heat the amine,
and it lets the gas go, so the carbon
dioxide can be pumped out of the boat and
the scrubber can be used again.
It's never removed completely. In data
reported in 2003,
carbon dioxide on US nuclear submarines
averaged around three and a half to four
thousand parts per million — several times
the level in outdoor air
with Navy exposure guidance setting
ceilings on how high it may rise.
That handles carbon dioxide. The oxygen
comes from water.
An electrolyser runs an electric current
through water and splits it into its two
ingredients: oxygen and hydrogen.
The oxygen goes into the air. The hydrogen
is explosive in enough quantity,
so on US submarines it's sent out of the
boat, into the sea.
Oxygen is held close to the level in
normal air:
too little dulls thinking, too much makes
fires more dangerous.
And there's a traditional chemical backup
oxygen candles,
which release oxygen as they burn.
Oxygen and carbon dioxide are only the
biggest of the air's problems.
Cooking, batteries, machinery and the crew
themselves all release other gases.
A catalytic burner removes carbon monoxide
and hydrogen,
and activated-charcoal filters soak up
odours and vapours.
A central analyser samples the air around
the clock,
tracking oxygen, carbon dioxide, hydrogen,
carbon monoxide and water vapour.
The same system air-conditions the boat:
in the living spaces of a US attack
submarine, it's designed for about eighty
degrees Fahrenheit
twenty-seven Celsius — and fifty percent
humidity.
Now the air is under control — but the
crew can't see where they're going.
There are no windows, and no GPS. GPS
works by radio,
and seawater soaks up radio; its signals
can't reach a submerged submarine.
So the boat keeps track of itself.
Gyroscopes sense every turn,
accelerometers sense every push and pull,
and a computer adds all of it up to work
out where the boat has moved.
The catch is that tiny errors add up too.
Left alone,
the estimate slowly drifts away from
reality.
So every so often the submarine checks its
position against something outside
for example, coming up near the surface
for a GPS fix,
or matching the shape of the seafloor
below to a map.
The exact methods vary between navies and
boats.
Knowing where you are only matters if no
one else knows.
A US Virginia-class submarine is three
hundred and seventy-seven feet long
about the length of a football field — and
it has to hide in water that carries sound
remarkably well.
Low-frequency sound loses very little
energy to absorption,
so low rumbles can be detected a long way
off; higher-pitched sounds fade much
sooner.
Many submarines are wrapped in special
coatings.
Some soak up incoming sonar pings, so less
sound echoes back.
Others muffle the noise the boat itself
makes.
None of this makes a submarine silent. It
makes it harder to hear
and harder to find.
Staying hidden creates the next problem:
how do you reach a submarine you can't
find? Seawater soaks up radio, and the
higher the frequency,
the faster it disappears.
Very-low-frequency radio does get in
but, according to the US Navy,
only tens of feet. To listen, a submarine
has to get an antenna up near the surface,
which limits how deep and how fast it can
go, and makes it easier to spot.
The US also ran an extremely-low-frequency
system,
at about seventy-six hertz. It could reach
submarines hundreds of feet down,
even while they were moving — but only one
way,
and slowly. It was shut down in 2004.
To reply, a submarine has to come near the
surface and use higher-capacity links,
such as satellite.
Every machine so far — the scrubbers, the
electrolyser,
the analysers, the navigation computers,
the sonar
runs on electricity. On this submarine,
that comes from a nuclear reactor.
Water in a sealed loop carries heat from
the reactor core to a separate system that
makes steam; the two waters never mix.
That steam spins turbines that make
electricity and help drive the boat.
The first nuclear submarine core lasted
about sixty-two thousand miles.
Today's submarine cores are rated for more
than a million.
So if the air, the course, the silence and
the power can all be managed,
what brings a nuclear submarine home?
Unlike surface warships,
submarines are almost never resupplied at
sea. Everything the crew will eat is
loaded before they leave.
Crews and machines need time ashore too:
US ballistic-missile submarines average
seventy-seven days at sea, then
thirty-five in port for maintenance,
with two full crews taking turns.
Food, maintenance, the people aboard and
the mission itself
those set the clock.
Outside, the ocean never changes. Inside,
every breath,
every course and every message depends on
a chain of hidden machines
each solving a problem the last one left
behind,
and all of them running on one source of
heat.
